props.title: Made in Heaven

sections.content: Made in Heaven (1987) represents a unique entry in the romantic fantasy genre, blending metaphysical concepts with earthbound love. Director Alan Rudolph, known for his unconventional narratives like Choose Me (1984), crafts a celestial romance that follows Timothy Hutton's Mike Shea, who dies heroically and finds himself in heaven where he falls in love with Kelly McGillis's Annie. The film shares thematic DNA with Defending Your Life (1991) and What Dreams May Come (1998) in its exploration of afterlife romance, but stands apart through its "second chance" narrative where the lovers must find each other again on Earth.

sections.content: The film's production design by Jeannine Oppewall creates a uniquely approachable vision of heaven, avoiding traditional religious imagery in favor of a more personal paradise. This approach influenced later films like A Life Less Ordinary (1997) and City of Angels (1998), which similarly reimagined celestial realms through contemporary lenses. The soundtrack, featuring original music by Mark Isham and songs by artists like Ric Ocasek and Ellen Shipley, creates a dreamy 80s atmosphere that enhances the film's romantic magical realism.

The second act's reincarnation plot draws fascinating parallels with other metaphysical romance films like Chances Are (1989) and Birth (2004). Hutton and McGillis's performances ground the fantastical elements in genuine emotion, while supporting appearances by Debra Winger and Neil Young (credited as Bernard Shakey) add quirky charm to the heavenly sequences. sections.content: Made in Heaven helped establish a template for supernatural romance films that would flourish in the 1990s. Its influence can be seen in movies like Ghost (1990) and Meet Joe Black (1998), which similarly explore love transcending mortality. The film's bold mixing of metaphysical concepts with romantic comedy elements paved the way for later genre-bending works like Prelude to a Kiss (1992) and Just Like Heaven (2005).
